(CNN) -- Scientists in Colombia have unearthed the remains of a true prehistoric monster believed to be the biggest snake ever to have lived on Earth. An artist's impression of what Titanoboa cerrejonensis would have looked like. Named Titanoboa cerrejonensis, the snake would have weighed 1,140 kilograms (2,500 pounds) and measured 13 meters (42.7 feet) nose to tail tip -- dwarfing the largest modern pythons and anacondas which can grow to 6 meters (19.5 feet). Scientists believe it slithered around the planet between 58 and 60 million years ago. Geologist David Polly, who identified the position of the fossil vertebrae which made a size estimate possible, said in a statement Wednesday: "At its greatest width, the snake would have come up to about your hips. The size is pretty amazing. "But our team went a step further and asked, how warm would the Earth have to be to support a body of this size?" Titanoboa's fossilized remains were discovered at a coal mine in the tropical Cerrejon region of northern Colombia by an international team of scientists. "Truly enormous snakes really spark people's imagination, but reality has exceeded the fantasies of Hollywood," paleontologist Jonathan Bloch, who co-led the expedition, told reporters. "The snake that tried to eat Jennifer Lopez in the movie 'Anaconda' was not as big as the one we found." Based on the snake's size, the team was able to calculate that the mean annual temperature in equatorial South America 60 million years ago would have been about 91 degrees Fahrenheit, about 10 degrees warmer than today, Bloch said. "Tropical ecosystems of South America were surprisingly different 60 million years ago," said Bloch. "It was a rainforest, like today, but it was even hotter and the cold-blooded reptiles were all substantially larger. "The result was, among other things, the largest snakes the world has ever seen...and hopefully ever will." According to Nature.com, snakes are poikilotherms (cold-blooded) that, unlike humans, need heat from their environment to power their metabolism. Therefore research suggests that at the time the region would have had to be no less than 86 to 93 degrees Fahrenheit for the snake to have survived. Most large snakes today live in the tropical regions of South America and south-east Asia, where the high temperatures allow them to grow to impressive sizes. Meanwhile, Carlos Jaramillo -- who was also part of the expedition -- said the tropical rainforest at Cerrejon appeared to have thrived at these temperatures. "This data challenges the view that tropical vegetation lives near its climatic optimum, and it has profound implications in understanding the effect of current global warming on tropical plants," he said.

Deep beneath the surface of northern Colombia, inside the sprawling, open-pit Cerrejón coal mine, paleontologists uncovered a window into a forgotten world. Among the layers of shale and rock exposed by heavy machinery, an international team of scientists made a startling discovery: fossilized vertebrae belonging to an ancient giant. 

Through meticulous analysis of these bone fragments, the researchers identified and reconstructed *Titanoboa cerrejonensis*, the largest snake ever discovered. But the significance of *Titanoboa* extends far beyond its terrifying dimensions. By calculating the physical and metabolic limits of this prehistoric behemoth, scientists gained unprecedented insights into the Earth’s climate 60 million years ago, proving that a scorching ancient environment paved the way for giant cold-blooded reptiles.

---

### Sizing Up a Monster

To understand the scale of *Titanoboa*, one must look at the mathematical relationship between the bones of modern constrictors and their overall body size. By comparing the fossilized vertebrae to those of living green anacondas and boa constrictors, the research team was able to extrapolate *Titanoboa’s* true dimensions.

The results were astonishing. *Titanoboa* stretched approximately 13 meters (43 feet) in length—longer than a modern city bus—and weighed an estimated 1,135 kilograms (1.25 tons). At its thickest point, the snake’s body would have reached up to a person's waist. It was an apex predator capable of crushing and swallowing giant crocodilians and massive prehistoric turtles in the swampy ecosystems it called home.

| Metric | *Titanoboa cerrejonensis* | Modern Green Anaconda |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Average Length** | ~13 meters (43 feet) | ~5 meters (16.5 feet) |
| **Estimated Weight**| ~1,135 kg (2,500 lbs) | ~100 kg (220 lbs) |
| **Era / Habitat** | Paleocene (60 Mya) / Swamps | Present / Amazon Basin |

---

### The Physiology of Heat and Growth

*Titanoboa’s* massive size presented a physiological puzzle: How could a cold-blooded creature grow so large?

Unlike warm-blooded mammals, which generate their own body heat through internal metabolic processes, reptiles are ectotherms (cold-blooded). Their body temperature, metabolic rate, and ultimate physical growth are dictated directly by the temperature of their surrounding environment. 

In colder environments, a giant cold-blooded animal would simply be unable to absorb enough ambient heat to power its metabolism and sustain basic bodily functions. Conversely, in a hotter climate, a reptile's metabolic engine runs faster, allowing it to process food more efficiently and grow to much larger physical proportions.

By applying thermodynamic models that correlate ambient temperature with reptile metabolism and body size, the researchers worked backward from *Titanoboa’s* 13-meter length to estimate the climate of its habitat.

The team's calculations revealed that for *Titanoboa* to survive, its tropical South American home had to be significantly hotter than the region is today. The average annual temperature of the Paleocene rainforests of Cerrejón was estimated to be roughly **10 degrees Fahrenheit (5 to 6 degrees Celsius) warmer** than modern tropical South America.

Sixty million years ago—roughly six million years after the asteroid impact that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs—the Earth was experiencing a period of intense global warming. Tropical environments were not dried-up deserts, but hyper-dense, hot, and soggy rainforests. The equatorial mean annual temperature exceeded 86°F (30°C) to 90°F (32°C). 

These extreme, steam-bath conditions provided the precise ecological furnace required to fuel *Titanoboa’s* massive growth. 

```
[ Ancient Global Warming ] ➔ [ Higher Ambient Temps ] ➔ [ Accelerated Reptile Metabolism ] ➔ [ Evolution of Gigantism (*Titanoboa*) ]
```

---

### A Window Into the Past—and the Future

The discovery of *Titanoboa cerrejonensis* fundamentally reshaped our understanding of prehistoric life and climate history. Prior to this research, many paleontologists believed that tropical ecosystems during the Paleocene epoch were already at their maximum heat limit and might suffer biologically under further warming. *Titanoboa* proved that ancient tropical rainforests could not only survive under higher temperatures, but thrive—hosting giant ecosystems driven by extreme heat.

Ultimately, this ancient constrictor serves as a dramatic example of how profoundly planetary climate dictates the evolutionary boundaries of life on Earth. While the conditions that allowed *Titanoboa* to slither through the swamps of ancient Colombia have long since faded, its fossilized spine remains a powerful testament to a time when heat ruled the Earth—and allowed giants to walk, swim, and crawl across its surface.

**(CNN) —** Deep in the humid coal mines of northern Colombia, paleontologists have unearthed the fossilized remains of the largest snake ever known to exist—a 42-foot behemoth that weighed a staggering 2,500 pounds.

The extinct species, dubbed *Titanoboa cerrejonensis* (meaning "titanic boa from Cerrejón"), slithered through South American rainforests roughly 60 million years ago, in the epoch following the mass extinction of the dinosaurs. 

While the sheer size of the prehistoric predator is astounding, researchers say the discovery carries far greater scientific importance: it provides definitive proof that temperatures near the equator were once significantly warmer than they are today.

### A real-life nightmare

The discovery was made after an international team of scientists excavated several fossilized vertebrae at the massive Cerrejón open-pit coal mine. 

Measuring nearly 13 meters (42 feet) long and weighing over 1.1 metric tons, *Titanoboa* makes today’s largest modern snakes look modest by comparison. For context, the green anaconda—the world's heaviest living snake—rarely exceeds 20 feet in length and 500 pounds.

"This snake weighed more than a bison and was longer than a city bus," said the team of paleontologists behind the study. "At its thickest point, *Titanoboa* would have reached up to a person's waist."

Researchers believe the massive reptile was a non-venomous constrictor, spending much of its time in the water, hunting fish, giant turtles, and ancient crocodilians.

### Rewriting ancient climate history

Beyond its terrifying physical dimensions, *Titanoboa* is acting as a "paleo-thermometer" for climate scientists trying to reconstruct the Earth's past.

Because snakes are cold-blooded (ectothermic), they rely entirely on the ambient temperature of their environment to regulate their body heat and fuel their metabolism. In colder climates, cold-blooded animals remain small because there is simply not enough ambient heat to support a massive body mass. To grow to the titanic proportions of *Titanoboa*, the snake required a much warmer environment than exists in the tropics today.

By calculating the metabolic requirements of a 2,500-pound cold-blooded creature, researchers determined that the average annual temperature in equatorial South America 60 million years ago had to be significantly higher than modern temperatures—roughly 86°F to 93°F (30°C to 34°C), compared to today’s average tropical temperatures of around 80°F (27°C).

For years, scientists have debated whether the Earth's equatorial regions warmed up alongside the rest of the planet during historical greenhouse periods, or if the tropics possessed a natural cooling mechanism that capped temperatures. 

The existence of *Titanoboa* provides strong evidence for the former, proving that Earth’s tropical regions were capable of reaching much higher temperatures in the past—and supporting a flourishing, albeit giant, ecosystem in the process.

**SCIENCE DAILY** | SPECIAL REPORT

# Colossal Prehistoric Snake *Titanoboa* Reveals a Scalding Hot Ancient Earth

**By Science News Staff**

Deep within the open-pit coal mines of Cerrejón, Colombia, paleontologists have unearthed the fossilized remains of the largest snake ever known to slither across the Earth. Named *Titanoboa cerrejonensis*, this monster predator lived approximately 58 to 60 million years ago during the Paleocene epoch—a period of recovery following the catastrophic asteroid impact that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs.

Measuring an astounding 43 feet (13 meters) in length and weighing over 1.25 tons (1,100 kilograms), *Titanoboa* was a dominant apex predator of the ancient South American rainforest. But beyond its terrifying dimensions, the discovery is providing scientists with crucial, groundbreaking clues about the history of Earth's climate and the limits of animal physiology.

---

### A Creature Out of Hollywood

The discovery was made by an international team of scientists who stumbled upon giant vertebrae in the dusty strata of the Cerrejón mine. Initially mistaking the massive bones for those of a crocodile, closer anatomical inspection revealed the signature characteristics of a constrictor snake—though on a scale never before documented.

"Truly enormous snakes really spark people’s imagination, but this one exceeds the wildest dreams of Hollywood," said Dr. Jonathan Bloch, a vertebrate paleontologist at the Florida Museum of Natural History and co-leader of the expedition. "The snake that tried to eat Jennifer Lopez in the movie *Anaconda* wasn't as big as the one we found."

Bloch and his team quickly realized that *Titanoboa* was not just a marvel of natural history, but a living thermometer from a ancient Earth.

```
       [ Modern Green Anaconda ] ───~20 ft (6 meters)
       [  Titanoboa Fossil   ] ───────────────~43 ft (13 meters)
```

---

### The Science of Poikilotherms: Why Size Matters

To understand how *Titanoboa* grew to such gargantuan proportions, researchers had to look to the fundamental biology of reptiles. 

Unlike mammals and birds, which are endotherms (warm-blooded) and generate their own internal body heat, reptiles are **poikilotherms**—cold-blooded organisms whose internal body temperatures fluctuate in direct response to their surrounding environment. 

A poikilotherm relies entirely on ambient heat to drive its metabolic processes, including digestion, respiration, and circulation. Because larger bodies require significantly more energy and heat to function effectively, a cold-blooded animal can only reach massive physical sizes if the environment around it is sufficiently hot. 

If the environment is too cold, a giant reptile’s metabolic rate drops too low, making survival impossible. Therefore, the maximum attainable size of a poikilotherm is directly tied to the average annual temperature of its habitat.

Dr. David Polly, a paleontologist at Indiana University who conducted mathematical modeling linking reptile size to ambient temperatures for the study, emphasized this physiological boundary:

> "Because snakes are poikilotherms, their maximum body size is fundamentally limited by ambient temperature. To support a creature the size of *Titanoboa*, the tropics had to be significantly warmer than they are today. The physics and metabolic demands are non-negotiable—a cold environment simply cannot host a snake of that mass."

---

### Climate Implications: A Window into a Super-Warmed Tropics

By analyzing *Titanoboa*’s biological requirements, scientists derived a revolutionary paleoclimate metric. The presence of the giant snake indicates that the equatorial region of Paleocene South America was far hotter than previously thought.

Based on *Titanoboa*’s mass, the research team calculated that the average annual temperature in the Paleocene neotropics was roughly **30°C to 34°C (86°F to 93°F)**. This is significantly warmer than modern tropical temperatures, which average around 26°C to 28°C (79°F to 82°F).

This finding sparked intense debate among climate scientists. Prior to the discovery of *Titanoboa*, some paleoclimate models suggested that equatorial regions possessed a natural "thermostat" mechanism—a ceiling that prevented the tropics from overheating during historical periods of intense global warming. *Titanoboa* shattered that hypothesis, demonstrating that as global temperatures rise, the tropics warm up alongside the rest of the planet.

Dr. Carlos Jaramillo, a paleobotanist at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and co-leader of the research project, highlighted the ecological reality of this ancient warm period:

> "Cerrejón gives us a unique window into the first neotropical rainforest after the extinction of the dinosaurs. The discovery of *Titanoboa* shows us that a warmer world hosted a vibrant, albeit radically different, tropical ecosystem. It proves that the tropics were far from immune to global heating—they changed dramatically."

### Looking Back to See Ahead

The story of *Titanoboa* is more than an ancient monster tale. As human greenhouse gas emissions continue to warm the planet, understanding how past ecosystems responded to elevated temperatures is critical for predicting future climate shifts.

While modern snakes are unlikely to evolve into 40-foot giants anytime soon—a process that requires millions of years of evolutionary pressure—*Titanoboa* serves as a striking reminder of how intimately life and climate are interwoven. Earth's distant, scorching past may well offer a preview of the dynamic, unpredictable world of tomorrow.
